The reasoning correctly shows that for any odd prime \(p\ge 3\) the only possible factorisation would have two monic degree‑\(p\) factors whose reductions modulo \(p\) are \((x-1)^p\) and \((x+1)^p\).  A detailed coefficient comparison forces \(m=p\) and then leads to an impossible monomial identity, so no admissible triples exist for odd primes.

For \(p=2\) the conditions reduce to \(n\in\{1,3\}\) and \(m\in\{1,2,3\}\setminus\{n\}\).  Direct verification shows that exactly the four listed triples give reducible polynomials, with the given factorizations.

Summing the values of \(p+m+n\) over these four triples yields \(5+6+6+7=24\).

Hence the final answer 24 is correct.
